question: On a flat road, how much of a cyclist's effort goes into pushing air rather than rolling the bike?
answer: Most of it, above a gentle pace. Air drag grows with the square of speed while rolling resistance barely changes: for a typical rider on the hoods, air takes half the effort at 15 km/h and four fifths at 30. The rider's body makes most of that drag, so a lower torso beats a lighter frame.
move: Find the biggest force against you before paying to shrink a small one.
ask: Am I spending on the small thing that is easy to buy, instead of the big thing I could change myself?
source: Faria et al., 2005; Martin et al., 1998
reference: Faria, Parker & Faria, The science of cycling: factors affecting performance, part 2, Sports Medicine, 2005; Martin, Milliken, Cobb, McFadden & Coggan, Validation of a mathematical model for road cycling power, Journal of Applied Biomechanics, 1998

notes.text: Walking pace: the tyres take most of the effort.
15 km/h, an easy ride: already half the effort pushes air.
30 km/h: four fifths is air. A kilo off the bike saves well under 1%.
Racing speed: nine tenths is air, most of it met by the rider's body.
